hero.title: Swim, play, *pause*
hero.lede: A saltwater pool with eight lap lanes, six courts for tennis and pickleball, and a 1929 gymnasium, on the grounds of the old Fermata School in the heart of Aiken.

image.alt: The Fermata pool at sunset, the still water reflecting an orange sky

sections.title: Take a pause *with us*
sections.intro: A fermata is a musical sign to pause and hold a note longer than usual: an apt name for a place to slow down with family and friends.

items.title: Saltwater pool
items.text: Eight 25-yard lap lanes and a diving area, plus a 1½-foot wading pool for the youngest swimmers.

items.title: Tennis & pickleball
items.text: Five tennis courts and two pickleball courts with moveable nets, shaded by longleaf pines and oaks.

items.title: Historic gymnasium
items.text: Built in 1929 for the Fermata School for Girls, and the home of the club’s holiday parties.

items.title: Swim team & lessons
items.text: A competitive swim team and Red Cross Learn to Swim classes of up to six.

items.title: Leagues & clinics
items.text: Home to CSRA and USTA league teams, with weekly clinics and private lessons.

items.title: Parties & events
items.text: Pool parties, gym rentals and socials like Twist, after Sunday Funday tennis.

sections.title: From the Fermata School *to a family club*

image.alt: A white two-story building from the Fermata School days, behind blooming azaleas

body: The club stands on the grounds of the Fermata School for Girls, founded in 1919 by the internationally famous pianist Josef Hofmann and his wife, Marie Eustis Hofmann, for the young women of Aiken’s Winter Colony. A fire in 1944 left only the gymnasium and the headmaster’s home and infirmary.

In 1952, 16 families leased and later bought the property to form a social club; by the end of that summer there were 116. It is still member-owned, and the Fermata Foundation, a 501(c)(3), works to preserve the 1929 gymnasium.
